title: The Loving
hook: one of God's names in the Quran: the Loving
carry: love that is warm and shows

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thérèse and her flowers. Your line was a grain of sand. Which ordinary thing did you do with love inside it? Today we turn to Muslim and Sufi voices, and a name. Day eight hundred thirty-six.

The Quran calls God by name after name. The Merciful. The Wise. The Hearing. The Seeing. In Muslim practice they are recited and reflected on, and some parents give them to their children, joined to the word Abd, servant: Abd al-Rahman, servant of the Merciful. One of the names is soft enough that it can catch a listener off guard. It isn't power, or knowledge, or judgment. It's warmth. Al-Wadud. The Loving. Today: where that name appears, and what sits right next to it.
screen: `GOD'S NAMES IN THE QURAN.` → `SERVANT OF THE MERCIFUL.` → `ONE NAME IS WARMTH.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Tradition links al-Wadud to wudd, an Arabic word for affection: not a distant goodwill, but love that is warm and shows. Elsewhere the Quran says that for those who believe and do good, the Merciful will appoint love, using that same word. Love, in this picture, is something God gives and also places between people. Second, the neighbors. The name appears in the chapter called al-Buruj, the Constellations, and Pickthall translates it like this: "And He is the Forgiving, the Loving." Forgiving and Loving, side by side. Some readers notice the order: forgiveness first, and then a love that is still there afterward, not a pardon given at arm's length. Third, the setting, which is the surprise. That chapter opens with a terrible story, the people of the ditch, a fire, and believers tormented only because they believed. A few verses later, the punishment it warns of is for those who persecute and "repent not." Some commentators point to those words: even for people that cruel, a door is described as still open. And right after comes the name: the Forgiving, the Loving. In another chapter the prophet Shuayb tells his people to ask pardon and turn back, and says, "Lo! my Lord is Merciful, Loving." Again, love beside mercy. Fourth, a Sufi voice. People tell a story about Rabia of Basra, an early woman mystic, carrying a torch and a bucket of water through the streets: to burn paradise and put out hell, she said, so that God would be loved for God alone. It's a story told, not a text. But it points at the same name.
screen: `WUDD: LOVE THAT SHOWS.` · `THE FORGIVING, THE LOVING.` · `A DOOR LEFT OPEN.` · `RABIA'S TORCH AND BUCKET.` · then, large: `AL-WADUD.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself who could use a loving word today. Maybe someone you've had to forgive, or who has had to forgive you. Picture them. Now find one warm word, or a few, that you could actually say: I'm glad you called. Thank you for waiting for me. It's good to see you. Let it be simple and true. If you pray, you can call on God as al-Wadud, the Loving, in your own way. Then rest. The bell holds the time.
Al-Wadud. The Loving: one of God's names in the Quran, love that is warm and shows, set right beside the Forgiving. Today's word.
Your line: love that is warm and shows. Today, say that one warm word out loud to the person you pictured. Day eight hundred thirty-six.

screen: `DAY 836 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT YOU'D WANT FOR YOURSELF.`

howItsDone: Muslims call on God by His names in prayer and remembrance, and some reflect on one name at a time, such as al-Wadud, the Loving, and try to show something of it in how they treat others.

fork.setup: a chapter of the Quran tells of the people of the ditch, who tormented believers beside a fire. a few verses later, which names of God follow?
fork.reveal: the Forgiving, the Loving. after a story of cruelty, the chapter names forgiveness and warm love.

original.note: Arabic: the Loving, one of God's names in the Quran, linked by tradition to wudd, affection.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gentle title for God.
what it means: al-Wadud, love that is warm and shows, named right beside forgiveness.
what a scholar hears: in al-Buruj it follows the story of the people of the ditch and a warning to those who "repent not": the door named as open, then the Loving.

notes: Pickthall wording to verify: 85:14 'And He is the Forgiving, the Loving'; 85:10 '...and repent not...'; 11:90 'Lo! my Lord is Merciful, Loving.'
Wadud from wudd ('affection'): standard lexicon gloss; confirm. 19:96 paraphrased as the Merciful appointing love (wudd) for believers who do good; confirm.
'Some commentators' reading the 'repent not' of 85:10 as a door left open: attributed; confirm a Keeper is comfortable.
Rabia's torch and bucket is presented explicitly as a story people tell, not a sourced text; 'early woman mystic' given without a date. Confirm.
Theophoric names (Abd al-Rahman) given as an example of how names are used; confirm wording 'some give them to their children'.
The Prophet Muhammad is not named in this script, so no honorific is needed; Shuayb is named as a prophet per 11:84–95.
Editor: 'many names' to 'name after name'; the wudd root is now 'tradition links' (claims rule on etymology), in teach and original note; varied the practice opener.
Audit: 'The Patient' (al-Sabur) is in the traditional list of 99 names but is not used as a name in the Quran itself; replaced with 'The Seeing' (al-Basir), which is Quranic.
